turns.finalMessage:
This is a bounded fix. My understanding: bulk renames must never stop after partially modifying the directory; collisions should be detected before any files move, including collisions within the generated plan. Existing names must not be overwritten.

When any collision exists, should the command:

1. Abort the entire run before changing anything, with a clear diagnostic (recommended), or
2. Skip conflicting entries and rename the rest?

Design:

- `planRenames` remains responsible only for producing the ordered rename plan.
- `applyRenames` performs a complete preflight before moving anything:
  - Identify targets already present in the directory, excluding exact no-op steps where `from === to`.
  - Identify duplicate targets generated within the plan.
  - If clashes exist, throw one clear error listing every conflicting target and its source entry or entries.
  - Only execute renames after the entire plan passes validation; never overwrite or skip.
- `src/cli.js` will catch the validation error, print its message to stderr, and exit nonzero. Planned moves may still be printed to stdout as today.
- Tests will use isolated temporary directories and verify existing-target clashes, duplicate planned targets, zero partial renames, clear clash listings, and successful collision-free renames.

Assumption: an exact `from === to` entry is harmless and treated as a no-op, not a clash. All other pre-existing targets abort the run, even if that target is also scheduled as a source.

Does this design look right?

You’re right; the design needs a transactional rename protocol, not only validation.

Revised design:

- Build a case-insensitive directory snapshot and validate the complete plan before changing anything.
- Treat only exact `from === to` entries as no-ops. If names differ only by case, report a clash.
- Exclude no-ops from execution, which makes an identical second invocation complete successfully without filesystem changes.
- Reject duplicate targets and targets occupied by files outside the moving source set, listing every clash.
- Execute valid plans in two phases using unique temporary names in the same directory:
  1. Move every source to its temporary name.
  2. Move every temporary file to its final target.
- If either phase fails, roll back all completed moves in reverse order so every source regains its original name.
- Print clash or filesystem diagnostics to stderr and exit nonzero.
- Tests will inject failures during both phases and verify restoration, alongside collision, case-only clash, duplicate-target, successful-run, and second-run no-op coverage.

One platform limitation needs an explicit decision: ordinary filesystem APIs cannot guarantee restoration if rollback itself fails—for example, the disk disconnects or permissions change mid-rollback. Should the contract be “restore all originals when rollback operations remain possible, and clearly report any rollback failure”? That is the strongest guarantee available without a journal/recovery mechanism, which the README declares out of scope.

Implemented transactional bulk renaming.

- Preflights all case-insensitive clashes before changes.
- Lists every existing or duplicate target conflict.
- Uses temporary names for two-phase renaming.
- Restores original names after filesystem errors whenever possible.
- Reports rollback failures and files needing manual attention.
- Treats exact repeat runs as no-ops.
- Rejects case-only clashes and occupied directory names.
- CLI diagnostics go to stderr with a nonzero exit code.

userReplies: 1. Abort the entire run before changing anything, and clearly list the clashes. Do not skip entries or overwrite anything.

Not yet. Preflight alone does not prevent a filesystem error during the moves from leaving the directory half-renamed. The run must either complete entirely or restore every original name. Also verify that running the same command twice makes the second run a no-op. Treat case-only clashes as clashes on this machine.
Yes, use that contract. Restore everything whenever possible, and clearly report any rollback failure and which files may need attention.
